name: Hana Rossi

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, and your name won't be attached to any of it. Could you start by telling me a little about yourself?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Hana, I'm 27, and I work on the acute medical admissions unit at Harbourside Hospital, which is where people come up from the emergency department before they get a proper ward bed. I qualified with a two-year diploma about eighteen months ago. I live on my own in a small flat two streets from the hospital; my parents helped with the deposit, and the mortgage is nearly paid off.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does a normal working day look like for you? What do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Admissions is fast. You get someone up from the emergency department, you do their obs, their bloods, their drug chart, and four hours later they're gone to a ward and you've got someone new. I love the pace and I love that every patient is a puzzle. What wears me out is that I'm still not quick at spotting when someone is getting worse, so I use AI tools on my phone a lot to check guidelines and practise drug sums on my break.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, honestly, that's a shame, because the bits that work are really useful. I'd post about the voice-notes pilot we ran on admissions, because it saved me about forty minutes a shift. I'd tell people not to throw away the small wins just because the big promises didn't happen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be fine. My job was never going to be taken by a chatbot, and I'd keep using the small tools to cover my weak spots. I'm still slow with clinical judgement, and having something to check a guideline at speed helps me more than the seniors realise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working on admissions and keep pushing the voice-notes tool to the other wards, maybe as the ward's tech champion. I'd do my cannulation training properly, which is putting drips into veins, because I still miss more than I should. Money stays as it is; the mortgage is small and I've got about eight months saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with a bit of disappointment. I like new things, and this would be a world with fewer of them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're slow with clinical judgement. What does that look like on a busy shift?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last week a woman came in with what looked like a chest infection, and I didn't spot that her blood pressure was sliding until my senior, Kwame, asked me about it. I'd had the numbers right in front of me. So yes, I use the AI tools to cover my gaps, but the gaps are mine to fix.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would anyone at work be glad AI stayed small?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Plenty. Our healthcare assistant Doreen has been here twenty years and hates every screen they give her. She'd be thrilled. I'd be glad for her, honestly, even if I'm a bit bored.

say: I'd say it's a **shame**, because the small tools really do help.
I'd post about our **voice-notes pilot**, which saved me forty minutes a shift.
think: My job was **never at risk** from a chatbot.
I'd keep using AI to cover my **weak spots**, like checking guidelines fast.
do: Push the **voice-notes tool** to other wards as the ward's tech champion.
Do the **cannulation training** properly, because I still miss veins.
Leave my **eight months of savings** and small mortgage as they are.
feel: **Calm**, with a little **disappointment** at a world with fewer new things.
S0.quote: I use the AI tools to cover my gaps, but the gaps are mine to fix.
fieldNote: She openly admits **clinical gaps**, like missing a falling blood pressure.
She uses AI daily as a **safety net**, not a replacement for learning.
She'd be glad for **older colleagues** who hate screens, even if she's bored.

steps.text: Spread the voice-notes tool to other wards as tech champion
Complete the cannulation training on the admissions unit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a chance, if it's done fairly. I'd be the one at work saying, look, the handover summaries and the discharge letters can be drafted by the machine, and we check them. Online I'd be arguing that hospitals should own these tools, not rent them from some company that can triple the price.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's good for me. I'm comfortable with the tools, and in a world where everyone has to learn them, being the person who already knows them is worth something. I'd worry more for the healthcare assistants, because robots for fetching and lifting will come for their jobs before mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply for a part-time role in nursing informatics, which means the nurses who help set up and fix the hospital's computer systems. I'd run training sessions for my ward on the new tools, on my own time if I had to. And I'd go to the union to push for the healthcare assistants to get paid retraining.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, even a bit excited. A little guilty about being excited, given what it means for other people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd feel guilty. Who would you feel it about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Doreen, mostly, and the other assistants. The healthcare assistants do the hardest physical work for the lowest pay, and they'll be the first ones a hospital tries to replace with a machine. If I'm getting a nice new job out of this while Doreen loses hers, that doesn't sit right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd train people on your own time. Is that realistic on top of a full rota?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For a few months, yes. I'm twenty-seven, no kids, and the flat is two streets from the hospital. I'd do a half-hour session after day shifts, with tea and biscuits, and see who turns up.

say: I'd say it's a **chance**, if machines draft the letters and nurses check them.
I'd argue online that **hospitals should own** these tools, not rent them.
think: Knowing the tools already makes me **valuable** when everyone must learn them.
**Healthcare assistants** will lose out to fetching and lifting robots before me.
do: Apply for a **part-time informatics** role setting up hospital computer systems.
Run **after-shift sessions** for my ward on the new tools.
Push the **union** for paid retraining for healthcare assistants.
feel: **Calm** and a bit **excited** about the new work.
**Guilty** that I'd gain while assistants like Doreen lose out.
S1.quote: The healthcare assistants do the hardest physical work for the lowest pay, and they'll be the first ones a hospital tries to replace with a machine.
fieldNote: She sees herself as a **winner** in this picture and says so plainly.
Her conscience is with **lower-paid assistants**, not with nurses like her.
Living two streets from the hospital, she has **time to give** freely.

steps.text: Apply for a part-time nursing informatics role at the hospital
Run half-hour after-shift training sessions on the new tools
Push the union for paid retraining for healthcare assistants

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need a public plan right now: a guaranteed income while people retrain, and rules on what a hospital can hand to a machine. I'd be organising, not just posting, because two years leaves no room for waiting. I'd probably start a group chat for nurses who want to push the union on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it flips my plans. I'd been thinking of moving into hospital computer systems work, but if AI can do any thinking work by 2028, that's the first thing to go. The hands-on bit of nursing, the cannulas and the washes and holding someone's hand, buys me until about 2031. So the boring advice I'd give anyone else is the one I'd take: stay at the bedside and get good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd drop the informatics idea straight away and put everything into clinical skills: cannulation, sepsis care, and a course in acute care. I'd use every AI tool I can in the first two years to learn faster, like a tutor in my pocket. And I'd join the union's campaign properly, maybe as a rep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I'm not scared for my bills, because the flat is nearly paid off. I'm unsettled because the plan I liked just disappeared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would happen to your savings in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep them, and maybe pay off the last bit of the mortgage early so there's nothing hanging over me. Eight months of savings plus no mortgage means I could ride out a lot. That's a lucky place to be at twenty-seven, and I know it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd use AI as a tutor. Isn't that the same AI that's coming for jobs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, and I see the joke. But refusing it wouldn't stop it, it would just make me slower. I'd rather use the thing to get good enough that the hospital keeps me when the robots arrive in 2031.

say: I'd call for a **public plan** now: guaranteed income while people retrain.
I'd start a **nurses' group chat** to push the union, because two years is no time.
think: AGI by 2028 kills my plan to move into **computer systems work**.
**Hands-on nursing** buys me until about 2031, so I'd stay at the bedside.
do: Drop the informatics idea and take an **acute care course**.
Use AI daily as a **pocket tutor** to learn clinical skills faster.
**Pay off** the last bit of my mortgage early.
feel: **Uneasy**, because the plan I liked has disappeared.
**Secure** about money, with the flat nearly paid off.
S2.quote: I'd been thinking of moving into hospital computer systems work, but if AI can do any thinking work by 2028, that's the first thing to go.
fieldNote: Short warning **reverses her career plan**: the desk role now looks least safe.
She sees the **irony** of using AI to stay ahead of AI, and accepts it.
Her **money cushion** removes fear; her unease is about direction, not survival.
She'd move from posting to **organising** colleagues.

steps.text: Drop the informatics plan and enrol on an acute care course

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time to do this fairly, and I'd hold the government to it. I'd write about it online, especially about healthcare assistants and cleaners, who'd be hit by robots in 2034. At work I'd be saying, let's learn the tools now so we're the ones shaping them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd be all right. Thinking AI by 2031 still kills the informatics idea in the long run, but it gives me a few years in it first, which would teach me how hospitals actually buy and use this stuff. Then I'd go back to the bedside before 2034 with skills most nurses don't have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do a year or two in informatics part-time while keeping some shifts on admissions. I'd do a degree top-up, because a diploma won't be enough for the senior jobs that are left. And I'd push my union branch to set up a fund for assistants to retrain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Busy and a bit stretched, but calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why go into informatics if you know it disappears by 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because for a few years that's where the decisions get made. If I'm on the hospital computer team in 2027, I can argue for nurses before the robots are bought, not after. Then I'd walk back to the ward with my eyes open.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your parents about it? They helped with the flat.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum would tell me to stop chasing shiny things and stick to nursing. I'd tell her I am sticking to nursing, just taking a detour. She'd roll her eyes and then ask if I'm eating properly.

say: I'd say **five years** is enough to do this fairly, and hold government to it.
I'd write about **assistants and cleaners**, who'd face robots in 2034.
think: A few years in **informatics** would teach me how hospitals buy technology.
I'd return to the **bedside** before 2034 with rare skills.

Start a **degree top-up**, since a diploma won't reach senior jobs.
Push my union branch to set up a **retraining fund** for assistants.
feel: **Calm**, though busy and a bit stretched.
S3.quote: If I'm on the hospital computer team in 2027, I can argue for nurses before the robots are bought, not after.
fieldNote: With five years, she treats informatics as a **planned detour**, not a destination.
She wants to be in the room **before robots are bought**.
Her concern for **lower-paid staff** stays constant across the pictures.

steps.text: Take a part-time hospital informatics post while keeping admissions shifts
Start a part-time nursing degree top-up
Push her union branch to set up a retraining fund for assistants

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, and wasting it would be a scandal. I'd talk about it as a plan for the whole health workforce, not a tech story. I'd probably write something long online that nobody reads.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be excited. Ten years is a whole career stage: I could do informatics properly, then a master's maybe, and be one of the people deciding how robots work on wards in 2039. The one risk is me getting lazy because it feels far away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go into informatics part-time within the year and stay in it for several years. I'd start a degree top-up and think about a master's later. And I'd set myself a check-in each January to ask whether the dates are moving faster than promised.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and excited. A bit like the start of a long trip.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the risk is getting lazy. Has that happened to you before?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. I meant to do my cannulation sign-off for a whole year and kept putting it off because nothing forced me. Ten years is that times a hundred. So I'd write the January check-in into my calendar and actually keep it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change anything about your personal life with ten years' warning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much. I'd maybe think about having kids around thirty-three, once I'm settled in a senior role. The flat would be paid off, and that's the main thing.

I'd frame it as a **workforce plan** for health care, not a tech story.
think: I could build a **whole career stage** around shaping ward robots by 2039.
My main risk is **getting lazy** because the date feels far off.

Start a **degree top-up**, with a master's later.

fieldNote: She knows her weakness is **procrastination**, shown by a delayed cannula sign-off.

steps.text: Move into part-time informatics work within the year

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, not for my money but because it wipes out every plan at once and leaves the assistants with nothing. What would help is a guaranteed income while people retrain, and a rule that hospitals can't buy a robot without a plan for the person whose job it takes. I'd also want the tools publicly owned, so a company can't hold a hospital to ransom.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who decides. Right now nurses aren't in the room when hospitals buy new technology, and the assistants and cleaners who'd lose most definitely aren't. I'd want that to change before anything else does.

headlineQuote: Right now nurses aren't in the room when hospitals buy new technology, and the assistants and cleaners who'd lose most definitely aren't.
portrait: Hana, 27, is a **junior nurse** on an acute admissions unit who uses AI every day.
She owns a **nearly paid-off flat** near the hospital, lives alone and has eight months saved.
She admits **clinical gaps** and uses AI as a tutor and safety net.
Her plan to move into **informatics** collapses under fast AGI, sending her back to the bedside.
Her strongest feelings are for **healthcare assistants**, who she thinks will lose first.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because it erases her plans and leaves assistants with nothing.
whatWouldHelp: A **guaranteed income** while people retrain, and rules tying robot purchases to job plans.
